source.title: Large Multi-modal Models Can Interpret Features in Large Multi-modal Models
source.authors: Kai-Chen Zhang; Yi-Fei Shen; Bo Li; Ziwei Liu

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies SAE feature discovery and evaluation to large multimodal models and reports results in that new setting. It does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates SAE-derived feature explanations using IoU, CLIP score, and GPT-4o/human consistency scores, including comparisons with random baselines. It also reports steering examples and hallucination-steering results, but those assess deliberate interventions rather than whether the claimed representational geometry occurs without intervention, so they are not recorded as rows for these versions. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study trains TopK SAEs on a new kind of system, LMMs (LLaVA-NeXT-8B, InstructBLIP-7B, Qwen2.5-VL). It reports that SAE features' top-activating image regions match one coherent concept well above a random-image baseline. That bears on V4's claim that a dictionary can recover sparse features in real models. The evidence is weak, because it is mediated by the authors' own auto-explanation pipeline. There is also no comparison against neurons and no reconstruction or sparsity statistics.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs plus an LMM-based auto-explanation pipeline can interpret open-semantic features in LMMs, that these features can steer behaviour and help localise errors such as hallucination, and that the results generalise across layers and architectures. They call it an initial step and note the limits of single-model, single-layer focus and of the cached image set.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK SAEs on LMM activations and evaluates feature explanations; it does not use the original toy-network setup or test sparsity-dependent superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported feature-interpretation scores vary across concepts and hook layers. The authors report better IoU and CLIP scores at greater layer depth in the tested cross-layer analysis.
record.code_released: GitHub codebase and checkpoints are stated to be open-sourced, but no URL is stated in the text.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The authors focus mainly on one model and one layer. They report results for a 5000-feature subset and around 46684 cached images, and state that the cache was not sufficiently large or diverse to interpret image features accurately; some features may have been misclassified as inactive. Cross-layer and cross-architecture evaluations are limited. The reported metrics assess explanation alignment/consistency, not feature completeness or stability.
record.rows_left_out: Table 10 is omitted because its flattened values cannot be reliably assigned to the displayed model and metric columns. The InstructBLIP-7B CLIP-score comparison is retained from Table 4; Table 10 appears to repeat it. Steering and hallucination-steering examples are omitted because they measure effects of deliberate feature clamping rather than the uninduced representation claims.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity or importance sweeps, no geometry, no phase transition.
No test of whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition, and no dedicated-dimension analysis.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No measurement of how features are distributed across neurons. No comparison of SAE features against neurons for interpretability. No reconstruction or variance-explained figures.
Completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, and canonicality are not tested. The paper only notes no loss decrease when going from 2^17 to 2^18 features.
The dimensionality of features is not examined.

missing.what: Qwen2.5-VL pipeline results: IoU 26.67 vs random 0.06 (scale apparently percent), CLIP score 27.99 vs random 18.22. Table 10 also repeats the InstructBLIP result of 28.01 vs 17.71. The flattened table is readable enough to record Qwen.

record.verdict_notes: V4 names LLMs; LMMs built on an LLM backbone are treated here as a new setting (T3). The random baseline uses random images, not random features or neurons, so the rows show feature coherence but not that SAE features beat neurons. Steering (Table 9) and hallucination clamping (Table 11) are deliberate interventions and are correctly left out. The 'GPT-4o'/'Human' subjects in r15–r28 should be reassigned to LLaVA SAE features.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity and importance sweeps, overlap geometry, transitions, and whether extra features are dropped.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

The study evaluates SAE feature interpretation in LMMs, not feature distribution across neurons in LLMs. It does not measure how many neurons encode each feature or establish that SAE features exhaustively recover the model's features.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features are not tested.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

relationships.condition: LLaVA-NeXT-LLaMA3-8B layer 25 SAE (2^17 features, k=256), across concept categories and layers 8/25/32; InstructBLIP-7B middle layer
relationships.reason: IoU (0.10–0.39 vs ≤0.01 random) and CLIP score (mostly about 23–26 vs about 18 random) are well above baseline. GPT-judged consistency is 0.84–1.0 (r1–r11, r13–r15, r17, r19, r21, r23, r25, r27, r29–r35).
relationships.display_finding: Features reached IoU of 0.10–0.39 against at most 0.01 for random, and CLIP scores of mostly about 23–26 against about 18. GPT-judged consistency was 0.84–1.0.
